sections.h2: How is Connecticut organized for someone selling a house?
sections.html:
Connecticut is divided into 169 incorporated towns, and the town is the unit that matters for almost every step of a sale. Property is assessed by the town, taxed by the town and recorded in the town clerk's land records. Some towns also contain cities or villages inside them.

The state sits between New York on the west and Rhode Island on the east, with Massachusetts to the north and Long Island Sound to the south. The Connecticut River roughly bisects it and empties into the Sound between Old Saybrook and Old Lyme. Hartford is the capital, and Bridgeport is the largest city.

That layout means two houses of similar size can have very different tax bills, filing offices and timelines depending only on which town they sit in. Our city and town guides cover those local details, and this page covers the rules that are shared statewide.

sections.h2: Do Connecticut counties have a role in a home sale?
sections.html:
No. County government was abolished in Connecticut in 1960, and the eight legacy counties are now mostly geographic and statistical labels. According to the Wikipedia list of Connecticut counties, county sheriffs were abolished by a legislative act effective in 2000.

Nine planning regions run by councils of governments have been recognized as county equivalents for most federal funding and statistical purposes, since 2015 under state law and since 2022 under federal law. They coordinate neighboring towns, and they do not assess, tax or record property.

The practical point for a seller is simple. When you call about a tax bill, a deed or a lien, you call the town office, not a county office.

sections.h2: Which Connecticut cities and towns do sellers hear about most?
sections.html:
The larger places by population include Hartford, Bridgeport, New Haven, Stamford, Waterbury, Norwalk, Danbury, New Britain, Greenwich and Bristol. They sit mostly along the coastal highway corridor from the New York line to New London and up the Connecticut River valley, which contrasts with the rural northeast and northwest corners of the state.

That mix shapes a sale. A seller in a small rural town and a seller in a coastal city face the same state statutes, but the local office, the mill rate and the pool of buyers differ. Ask the town hall early about payoff figures and certificates.

sections.h2: Who assesses and bills property tax in Connecticut?
sections.html:
Each town does, through its assessor and its tax collector. Section 12-62 of the General Statutes requires every town to revalue real property on a five-year cycle, with the state prescribing a schedule for each revaluation zone beginning October 1, 2023.

If you think a value is wrong, you appeal to the town's board of assessment appeals. A person who is still aggrieved can apply to the Superior Court within two months after the date the notice of the board's action was mailed, under section 12-117a.

The tax collector sends the bill and tracks payments. Under section 12-146, the delinquent part of a tax carries interest at 18 percent per year from its due date, with a two-dollar minimum per installment that a town can choose to waive. Due dates and installment schedules differ by town, so ask the tax collector in your own town rather than assuming a calendar from another one.

sections.h2: What tax breaks and creditor protections exist statewide?
sections.html:
The legislature sets a menu of exemptions in section 12-81, and each town's assessor applies them. Three examples are fixed-dollar reductions in assessed value.

  • Blind residents: $3,000.
  • Veterans who served in wartime: $1,000.
  • Service members and veterans with disability ratings: $3,500.

There is also a creditor protection for the home itself. Under section 52-352b, a homeowner's primary residence is exempt from ordinary judgment collection up to $250,000 of fair market value less liens. The exemption does not defeat a mortgage, which is a consensual lien.

None of these changes how a sale works in a given town. They do change what is owed and what a creditor can reach, which is worth knowing before you pick a buyer.

sections.h2: How is the real estate conveyance tax set up?
sections.html:
The conveyance tax has a state part and a municipal part, and both come due when the deed is recorded. The base state rate is three-quarters of one percent of the price and the municipal rate is one-quarter of one percent, under section 12-494. Property that is not residential is taxed at a higher state rate of one and one-quarter percent, except unimproved land.

The Department of Revenue Services says the tax applies when the consideration equals or exceeds $2,000. The seller or the seller's attorney or agent files Form OP-236 with the town clerk, or through myCTREC when the town participates, and the clerk sends the state portion on to DRS. If a sale uses more than one deed, tax is computed on the total consideration.

Because each of the 169 towns has its own clerk, recording hours, fees for copies and online options differ. The DRS site lists a three-digit code for each town for use on the return.

sections.h2: Which sales are exempt from the conveyance tax?
sections.html:
The DRS list is long, and several items matter to sellers in trouble. The tax does not apply to a mortgage deed, to a deed between spouses or to a tax deed, and the list also covers a number of distressed situations.

  • A deed in lieu of foreclosure on the transferor's principal residence.
  • A transfer by court decree after foreclosure by decree of sale or market sale under section 49-24.
  • A principal residence sold for a price too low to pay the mortgages and the tax liens that rank ahead of them.
  • A principal residence with a crumbling foundation caused by pyrrhotite, for the first transfer after a professional engineer's written evaluation, if the owner is not receiving help from the Crumbling Foundations Assistance Fund.
  • The principal residence of a seller approved for property tax assistance under section 12-129b or 12-170aa, which is exempt from the state tax but not the municipal tax.

Every exemption has a number that goes on line 14 of the return, and a return that claims an exemption without a code is incomplete.

sections.h2: What should a Connecticut seller ask the town offices?
sections.html:
A short set of questions saves weeks. Call or visit three offices, and write down the answers for your closing attorney.

  1. Assessor: what is the current assessed value, when was the last revaluation, and which exemptions are on file for this address.
  2. Tax collector: what is the balance, what interest has accrued and what is the payoff figure for a given closing date.
  3. Town clerk: how are deeds recorded here, what are the fees and is the town on myCTREC for the conveyance return.

If the house has a mortgage, request a payoff from the lender at the same time. If there is a tenant, collect the lease and the deposit records, since the deposit moves to the new owner. Our guides on eviction and landlord and tenant law in Connecticut explain those pieces.

faqs.q: How many towns are there in Connecticut?
faqs.a: There are 169 incorporated towns in Connecticut. Each one assesses, taxes and records property on its own.

faqs.q: Does Connecticut have county property taxes?
faqs.a: No. County government was abolished in 1960, so property tax is billed by the town. Planning regions that act as county equivalents do not tax property.

faqs.q: Who do I contact to record a deed in Connecticut?
faqs.a: The town clerk in the town where the property sits records the deed. The seller files the conveyance tax return with the clerk or online through myCTREC if the town participates.

faqs.q: How often are Connecticut properties revalued?
faqs.a: Every town must revalue real property at least every five years under section 12-62, following a schedule the state sets by revaluation zone.

faqs.q: What is the Connecticut conveyance tax rate on a typical home sale?
faqs.a: The base rates are 0.75 percent for the state and 0.25 percent for the municipality. Other rates apply to non-residential property and some residential estates, so check section 12-494 or ask the town clerk.
